practical.title: Variables, Data Types, and User Input in C — Interactive Calculator Lab
practical.sourceActivity: Variables, Data Types, and User Input in C — Interactive Calculator Lab

tasks.title: Observe & Understand — Run the baseline calculator
tasks.narratorGuide: Hi Learner — we'll start by running a fully working calculator program so you can observe how variables, scanf, and printf interact. Notice the prompts, the use of & with scanf, and the cast used to produce a floating-point quotient. This baseline is our reference: later you'll make targeted changes and compare outputs. Pay attention to the safe guard around division-by-zero — that prevents undefined behaviour like modulo with zero. Next, we'll intentionally change one line to see what integer division looks like.

tasks.title: Modify & Experiment — See integer division by changing one line
tasks.narratorGuide: Great — now let's change just one line to observe a different behavior. Edit the quotient printf so it prints an integer quotient (no cast). Compile and run with the same inputs you used before. You'll see the decimal part disappear because C performs integer division when both operands are integers. This is a key pitfall for beginners and an important tool when you want whole-number results.

tasks.title: Build & Integrate — Add an average (floating-point) output
tasks.narratorGuide: Nice work discovering integer division. Next, let's extend the program by adding an average calculation: (num1 + num2) / 2. If you write (num1 + num2) / 2 you'll get integer division again. To produce a decimal average, divide by 2.0 or cast one operand to float. Add a single printf line to print the average with two decimal places. This shows how small edits and type choices let you add more informative output.

tasks.title: Verify & Extend — Test edge cases and compare float-based inputs
tasks.narratorGuide: Finally, run a few edge cases: try second operand zero to make sure the program avoids modulo/divide-by-zero errors, and try negative values. Then compile and run the float-based calculator to see how %lf and double variables allow decimal inputs and outputs. This comparison cements why choosing the right type at design time matters. Well done — you've observed, modified, extended, and verified behavior end-to-end.

safety.learnerWarning: This practical runs in an isolated workspace. Do not use real credentials or production resources.

cleanup.instructions: Discard the isolated workspace after completion.
